topic: Understanding the Physics Underpinning Nanoparticle Dispersion in Polymers Via Statistical Interrogation
title: Understanding the Physics Underpinning Nanoparticle Dispersion in Polymers Via Statistical Interrogation
session_title: Special Session In Honor of Prof. Thanos Panagiotopoulos 65th Birthday (Invited Talks)
program_title: Computational Molecular Science and Engineering Forum
symposium_title: Computational Molecular Science and Engineering Forum
abstract: Polymer/nanoparticle (NP) mixtures can either have well-dispersed or agglomerated NPs depending on the used casting common solvent. Here, we use traditional statistical methods and machine learning (ML) classification models to elucidate the critical underpinning variables determining this behavior. Building on two databases, one sourced from over the existing literature and one created in-house, we conclude that the interaction strength between NPs and the solvent dielectric constant can reliably predict NP dispersion states. Physics based models then point to the key roles of charge stabilization of the NPs and the ability for a polymer to form a bound layer on the NP in this context. Finally, we also analyze the differences between our two datasets, and comment on the importance of using controlled datasets when training ML models or otherwise performing statistical analysis.

topic: Computational Design of Peptides As Detectors, Sensors and Drugs
title: Computational Design of Peptides As Detectors, Sensors and Drugs
session_title: Special Session In Honor of Prof. Thanos Panagiotopoulos 65th Birthday (Invited Talks)
program_title: Computational Molecular Science and Engineering Forum
symposium_title: Computational Molecular Science and Engineering Forum
abstract: We describe our efforts to develop an efficient computational algorithm that searches for peptides that bind strongly and selectively to specific biomolecular targets, and to use that algorithm in the design of peptide-based detectors sensors, and drugs. The algorithm, PepBD, is an iterative procedure that involves as many as 100,000 sequence mutation moves and/or peptide backbone conformation moves to arrive at the peptide sequence and conformation that has the lowest binding energy to the target. The top scoring peptides are then further evaluated by performing explicit-solvent atomistic simulations of the peptide–target complex to determine their binding free energies. We describe the application of this method to two projects.

title: Staying the Course - Excursions in Adaptively Revealed Free Energy Surfaces

symposium_title: Computational Molecular Science and Engineering Forum
abstract: This will be a short recounting of the adventures of a nonlinear dynamics person trying to explore free energy surfaces in a data-driven manner. It is therefore a history of many collaborations along the way, from Gerhard Hummer and Dimitris Maroudas and Thanos Panagiotopoulos in the 2000 years at Princeton, via Andy Ferguson, Pablo Debenedetti --and a little Indiana Jones- later on, to Juan Bello Rivas, John Guckenheimer, current students (Anastasia Georgiou) and colleagues (Brandon Bukowski) at Hopkins.

topic: From Block Copolymers to Peptides and Lipids: A Journey Inspired By Professor Panagiotopoulos
title: From Block Copolymers to Peptides and Lipids: A Journey Inspired By Professor Panagiotopoulos
session_title: Special Session In Honor of Prof. Thanos Panagiotopoulos 65th Birthday (Invited Talks)
program_title: Computational Molecular Science and Engineering Forum
symposium_title: Computational Molecular Science and Engineering Forum
abstract: It was under Professor Panagiotopoulos’ gracious tutelage over two decades ago at Princeton University that I first gained an appreciation for the elegant simulation techniques pioneered by his research group. These sophisticated techniques afforded deep insights and mechanistic understanding of complex fluids and materials in ways that were not easily accessible through empirical experimentation alone. That experience was foundational and has since enabled me to complement experimental research with modeling and simulations through various collaborations across industry and academia throughout my career. In this talk, I will share examples of our research that combines molecular dynamics simulations with NMR spectroscopy to elucidate the behavior of peptide-lipid membranes relevant to the characterization of novel peptide therapeutics and nucleic acid delivery systems such as lipid nanoparticles.

topic: Understanding Solvation Phenomena of Natural Compounds and Ions Using Molecular Simulations
title: Understanding Solvation Phenomena of Natural Compounds and Ions Using Molecular Simulations
session_title: Special Session In Honor of Prof. Thanos Panagiotopoulos 65th Birthday (Invited Talks)
program_title: Computational Molecular Science and Engineering Forum
symposium_title: Computational Molecular Science and Engineering Forum
abstract: This talk will focus on two case studies in which molecular simulations are used in conjunction with experimental investigations to better understand solvation phenomena. The first example will discuss hydrotropy, in which a large plant-based phenolic compound, syringic acid, is induced to dissolve in water via the use of a hydrotrope. There is a competition between the affinity of the solute and the hydrotrope and the tendency of the hydrotrope to aggregate. Free energy calculations and a Kirkwood-Buff analysis help shed light on this process. The second example focuses on the use of cosolvents for dissolving ions in electrolyte solutions. Different solvation patterns are observed depending on the nature of the ions and solvents. This solvation behavior can have an impact on the resulting performance of batteries. Understanding solvation behavior enables one to tailor the electrolyte chemistry to improve battery lifetime and performance.
